meta.scope: Sourced facts for the Telos Earth-orbit scene. Every entry carries a source URL. kind = historical (happened / measured) or projected (planned, announced or modelled).

conventions.dates: ISO 8601. UTC unless the detail says otherwise. A month-only or year-only date means the source gives no finer date.
conventions.derived_values: Entries marked 'derived' were computed by the researcher from CelesTrak GP element sets (mean motion to semi-major axis, minus 6378.137 km equatorial radius), so altitudes are approximate means rather than published figures.

could_not_confirm: A published final-approach closing speed of 0.1 m/s for Crew Dragon. The design paper gives a contact speed of 8 cm/s; 0.1 m/s appears only in unofficial simulator guides.
Docking ports for Soyuz MS-29, Progress 95 and Progress 96 (NASA's visiting-vehicle page lists dates but not ports).
Any official SpaceX or FCC statement of a Starlink constellation size for 2030.
A dated 2026 launch target for Orbital Reef.
A firm launch date for the first Tiangong expansion module.
The ISS reentry location being called the 'Spacecraft Cemetery' in a NASA document. NASA names the South Pacific Oceanic Uninhabited Area around Point Nemo.
Floor passage of S. 933 (ISS to 2032). Only committee approval (4 March 2026) is confirmed.

iss_history.title: Zarya launches
iss_history.detail: The Russian-built Zarya module, the first piece of the ISS, launched on a Proton rocket from Baikonur.

iss_history.title: Unity launches on STS-88
iss_history.detail: Shuttle Endeavour carried Node 1 Unity, the first US-built element, and mated it to Zarya on 6 December 1998.

iss_history.title: Zvezda docks
iss_history.detail: Zvezda, launched 12 July 2000 on a Proton, docked automatically to Zarya's aft port and gave the station its first living quarters.

iss_history.title: Expedition 1 arrives; continuous habitation begins
iss_history.detail: Shepherd, Gidzenko and Krikalev, who launched 31 October on Soyuz TM-31, docked to Zvezda and opened the hatch, starting continuous human presence.

iss_history.title: Destiny lab attached (STS-98)
iss_history.detail: Atlantis crew used the shuttle arm to latch the US Destiny laboratory onto Unity, raising onboard living space by 41 percent.

iss_history.title: Harmony (Node 2) installed (STS-120)
iss_history.detail: Harmony, launched 23 October 2007, became the hub that links Destiny, Columbus and Kibo and later hosts both commercial-crew docking adapters.

iss_history.title: Columbus installed (STS-122)
iss_history.detail: ESA's Columbus laboratory was attached to Harmony's starboard side.

iss_history.title: Kibo pressurized module installed (STS-124)
iss_history.detail: Japan's Kibo pressurized module was installed on Harmony's port side.

iss_history.title: Tranquility and Cupola installed (STS-130)
iss_history.detail: Node 3 Tranquility arrived with the Cupola attached; the Cupola was moved to Tranquility's Earth-facing port a few days later.
iss_history.note: NASA's Tranquility page names Harmony as the host, but the STS-130 mission account and NSSDC give Unity's port side. Unity is the better-supported attachment point.

iss_history.title: Assembly completed with the final shuttle flights
iss_history.detail: STS-134 (May 2011, AMS-02) and STS-135 (July 2011, the last shuttle flight) finished US assembly and outfitting before the shuttle retired.
iss_history.note: Another NASA page says assembly was complete in 'the fall of 2011'. Russian modules (Nauka 2021, Prichal 2021-11-26) were added later.

iss_history.title: First commercial spacecraft berthed (Dragon COTS Demo C2+)
iss_history.detail: Dragon, launched 22 May on Falcon 9, was grappled by Canadarm2 and berthed to Harmony's Earth-facing port, the first commercial vehicle to reach the ISS.

iss_history.title: IDA-2 installed on Harmony forward
iss_history.detail: The first International Docking Adapter was installed on the forward end of Harmony in summer 2016.

iss_history.title: IDA-3 installed on Harmony zenith
iss_history.detail: Spacewalkers Hague and Morgan installed the second docking adapter on PMA-3 on Harmony's space-facing side.

iss_history.title: First crewed Crew Dragon docks (Demo-2)
iss_history.detail: Behnken and Hurley launched 30 May 2020 from LC-39A and docked Dragon Endeavour to Harmony's forward port; soft capture 14:16 UTC, hard capture 14:27 UTC.

iss_history.title: First operational crew rotation (Crew-1) docks
iss_history.detail: Crew-1 launched 15 November 2020 at 7:27 p.m. EST and Dragon Resilience docked at 11:01 p.m. EST on 16 November (17 November UTC), the first operational Commercial Crew mission.

iss_history.title: Prichal added, the most recent module
iss_history.detail: NASA lists Russia's Prichal docking node as the most recent module added to the station.

iss_history.title: Crewed Dragon flight count: 21 with Crew-13
iss_history.detail: Crew-13 is described as the 21st crewed orbital flight of a Crew Dragon (Demo-2, Crew-1 to Crew-13, Inspiration4, Ax-1 to Ax-4, Polaris Dawn, Fram2).
iss_history.note: The count comes from Wikipedia. The researcher's own tally of known flights also gives 21. Ax-5 (NET January 2027) and Vast-1 have not flown.

iss_history.title: People who have visited the ISS
iss_history.detail: NASA's overview page counts 298 individuals from 26 countries who have visited the station.

frame.title: Station axes used here (LVLH)
frame.detail: +X (V-bar) points along the velocity vector (the station's 'forward'), +Z (R-bar) points to nadir (Earth's centre), so zenith = -Z; +Y completes the frame along the orbit normal.

docking_ports.title: IDA-2: Harmony forward (+X, velocity direction)
docking_ports.detail: This adapter on PMA-2 at the forward end of Harmony is used by Crew Dragon and Cargo Dragon; Crew-13 docked here on 1 October 2026.

docking_ports.title: IDA-3: Harmony zenith (-Z, away from Earth)
docking_ports.detail: This adapter on PMA-3 on Harmony's space-facing side is the second commercial port; Crew-4 docked here on 27 April 2022.

docking_ports.title: Docking capacity
docking_ports.detail: NASA says up to eight spacecraft can be docked to the station at once.

approach_profile.title: Approach ellipsoid
approach_profile.detail: This is a 4 x 2 x 2 km ellipsoid centred on the ISS centre of mass with its long axis along the V-bar; entering it starts joint operations with ISS mission control.

approach_profile.title: Keep-out sphere (KOS), radius 200 m
approach_profile.detail: This is a sphere of 200 m radius centred on the station's centre of mass; vehicles may enter it only after a go decision, inside an assigned corridor.
approach_profile.note: The Planetary Society calls it '200 meters wide'. NASA SSP 50235 and the NASA CRS risk paper both define a 200 m radius.

approach_profile.title: Waypoint 0: about 400 m below the station
approach_profile.detail: On a typical Crew Dragon timeline, Waypoint 0 is a hold point 400 m below the ISS, reached after the go to enter the keep-out sphere.

approach_profile.title: Waypoint 1: about 220 m out on the docking axis
approach_profile.detail: Dragon moves onto the docking-port axis and holds about 220 m from the station.
approach_profile.note: Planetary Society Demo-2 coverage gives 150 m from the forward port, likely measured from the port rather than the station centre. https://www.planetary.org/articles/crew-dragon-docks

approach_profile.title: Waypoint 2: 20 m hold, then final approach
approach_profile.detail: Dragon holds 20 m from the port for a final go/no-go, then closes in; Crew-4 contact came about 5 minutes after leaving Waypoint 2.

approach_profile.title: Contact speed about 8 cm/s; soft then hard capture
approach_profile.detail: Dragon's soft-capture ring absorbs a design contact speed of 8 cm/s (about 0.08 m/s); after ring retraction, 12 hard-capture hooks latch to the IDA.
approach_profile.note: This corrects the ~0.1 m/s in the brief. On Demo-2, hard capture came 11 minutes after soft capture (14:16 to 14:27 UTC, 31 May 2020).

dimensions.title: Mass 419,725 kg
dimensions.detail: NASA gives the station's mass as 925,335 lb (419,725 kg).

dimensions.title: End-to-end 109 m; truss 94 m
dimensions.detail: The station spans 109 m end to end (also the solar-array wingspan); the integrated truss is 94 m and the pressurized modules are 67 m long.
dimensions.note: The brief's '109 m truss' mixes two figures: 109 m is the overall span, the truss itself is 94 m.

dimensions.title: Pressurized volume 1,005 m3; habitable 388 m3
dimensions.detail: NASA lists 35,491 cubic feet pressurized and 13,696 cubic feet habitable, excluding visiting vehicles.

orbit.title: Altitude about 415 to 424 km
orbit.detail: Derived: the CelesTrak element set for epoch 2026-10-26 05:01 UTC gives perigee about 415 km and apogee about 424 km.
orbit.note: NASA describes the operating altitude as about 415 km (257 miles). https://www.nasa.gov/faqs-the-international-space-station-transition-plan/

orbit.title: Inclination 51.63 deg
orbit.detail: The CelesTrak element set for epoch 2026-10-26 lists inclination 51.6337 deg.

orbit.title: Orbital period 92.96 min
orbit.detail: Derived: a mean motion of 15.4906 rev/day gives a 92.96-minute orbit, about 15.5 orbits a day. NASA rounds this to 'about 90 minutes, 16 orbits per day'.

iss_current_vehicles.summary: NASA lists five spacecraft attached as of 15 October 2026: Crew-13 Dragon, CRS-35 Cargo Dragon, Soyuz MS-29, Progress 95 and Progress 96. No Cygnus, HTV-X, Starliner or Dream Chaser was attached.

attached.title: SpaceX Crew-13 (Dragon), Harmony forward
attached.detail: Watkins, Delaney, Kutryk (CSA) and Teteryatnikov launched at 15:10 UTC from SLC-40 and docked the same day to Harmony's forward port; return is planned NET March 2027.

attached.title: SpaceX CRS-35 (Cargo Dragon), Harmony zenith
attached.detail: CRS-35 launched 13 October and docked 15 October carrying supplies and a new iROSA solar array; departure is NET November 2026.
attached.note: The port (zenith) and cargo details come from NASASpaceflight's 22 October roundup, which could not be fetched directly. https://www.nasaspaceflight.com/2026/10/iss-roundup-102226/

attached.title: Soyuz MS-29
attached.detail: Soyuz MS-29 launched and docked on 14 July 2026, carrying Dubrov, Kikina (Roscosmos) and Menon (NASA).

attached.title: Progress 95
attached.detail: Progress 95 launched 25 April and docked 27 April 2026.

attached.title: Progress 96
attached.detail: Progress 96 launched 16 September and docked 19 September 2026.

recent_departures_2026.title: Cygnus NG-24 released
recent_departures_2026.detail: Cygnus NG-24, captured 13 April 2026, was released by Canadarm2.
recent_departures_2026.note: NASA's visiting-vehicles page lists 10/9; another NASA summary reportedly gave 10/8.

recent_departures_2026.title: Crew-12 undocks
recent_departures_2026.detail: Crew-12 (Meir, Hathaway, Adenot, Fedyaev) undocked on 7 October and splashed down on 8 October 2026 after about eight months; it had docked 14 February 2026.

recent_departures_2026.title: HTV-X1 released
recent_departures_2026.detail: JAXA's first HTV-X cargo ship was released from the station.

upcoming.title: Boeing Starliner-1 (uncrewed cargo)
upcoming.detail: On 28 September 2026 NASA said the uncrewed Starliner-1 engineering flight could launch in December 2026 or January 2027, with crew returning on Starliner-2 by 2028.

upcoming.title: Dream Chaser Tenacity: free-flyer demo only
upcoming.detail: A September 2025 contract change dropped the ISS docking; the first flight is a free-flight demo targeted for late 2026 on Vulcan, with no confirmed launch date.

upcoming.title: Axiom Mission 5 (Ax-5)
upcoming.detail: The fifth private astronaut mission on Crew Dragon is targeted NET January 2027 for up to 14 days docked.

iss_end.title: Transition report: deorbit near Point Nemo
iss_end.detail: NASA's 2022 transition report planned the final reentry burn over the South Pacific Oceanic Uninhabited Area (SPOUA) around Point Nemo and budgeted for deorbit in January 2031.

iss_end.title: SpaceX wins US Deorbit Vehicle contract (up to $843M)
iss_end.detail: NASA picked SpaceX for a single-award USDV contract worth up to $843 million; NASA will own and operate the vehicle, and its launch will be bought separately.

iss_end.title: Deorbit method
iss_end.detail: Natural drag lowers the station first; once the crew has left, operators line up the ground track and command a large reentry burn into an uninhabited ocean area.

iss_end.title: Orbit lowering begins (early to mid-2028)
iss_end.detail: GAO reports that NASA expects drag plus Russian-segment reentry maneuvers to start lowering the station in early to mid-2028.

iss_end.title: USDV completed
iss_end.detail: GAO cites NASA's estimate that SpaceX will complete the deorbit vehicle, a Dragon with an enlarged propulsive trunk, in 2028.

iss_end.title: Go/no-go decision on deorbit vs extension
iss_end.detail: In 2027 NASA will assess whether to launch the USDV in 2029 or extend ISS operations.

iss_end.title: USDV launches and attaches to the ISS (mid-2029)
iss_end.detail: NASA plans to launch the US Deorbit Vehicle in mid-2029 and attach it to the station.
iss_end.note: The month is approximate; GAO says 'mid-2029'. No USDV launch vehicle had been announced.

iss_end.title: Final reentry burn (end of 2030 or early 2031)
iss_end.detail: The USDV performs the reentry burn that drives the ISS into a remote part of the ocean, where surviving pieces fall.
iss_end.note: GAO (17 June 2026) says 'end of 2030 or early 2031'. The 2022 transition report assumed January 2031 for budgeting.

iss_end.title: Senate committee bill would extend ISS to 2032
iss_end.detail: The Senate Commerce Committee approved S. 933 (NASA Authorization Act of 2026), which would extend ISS operations to 30 September 2032; it is not law.
iss_end.note: No full Senate or House passage was found as of October 2026.

iss_end.title: GAO: structure certified through 2028, gap risk unassessed
iss_end.detail: GAO found the ISS structure analysed as safe through 2028 (NASA expects it could last to the late 2030s), costing about $3B a year, and that NASA had not assessed the risk of a gap in crewed presence.

successor_stations.title: Vast Haven-1
successor_stations.detail: Vast's single-module station is 10.1 m long and 4.4 m wide (45 m3 habitable, 80 m3 pressurized), for 4 crew on 2-week visits, in a 425 km, 51.6 deg orbit; it launches on Falcon 9.
successor_stations.note: This has slipped from August 2025, then May 2026; Ars Technica reported the move to Q1 2027 in January 2026. https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/01/the-first-commercial-space-station-haven-1-is-now-undergoing-assembly-for-launch/

successor_stations.title: Vast Haven-2
successor_stations.detail: Vast plans 16 m by 4.4 m modules launched on Falcon Heavy, the first operational in 2028, with a 9-module, 12-crew station (1,160 m3 pressurized) complete in 2032.
successor_stations.status: projected; depends on NASA commercial-station award

successor_stations.title: Axiom Station: PPTM attaches to ISS, then free-flies
successor_stations.detail: Axiom's first module, the Payload Power Thermal Module, attaches to the ISS and later separates to join Habitat 1 as a two-module free-flyer.
successor_stations.note: Axiom (25 September 2025) said PPTM launches 'toward the end of 2027' and could be free-flying as early as 2028, with four modules by 2030. Later 2026 reporting puts PPTM in 2028 and the habitat in 2029 (e.g. https://spacenews.com/axiom-space-raises-additional-350-million/), so treat 2027 as optimistic.

successor_stations.title: Starlab (Voyager / Airbus JV)
successor_stations.detail: Starlab is a single 8 m module with three decks, launched fully outfitted on one Starship, for 4 permanent crew (8 during handovers) at about 400 km.
successor_stations.status: passed NASA Commercial Critical Design Review on 2026-02-23; launch scheduled 2029

successor_stations.title: Orbital Reef (Blue Origin / Sierra Space)
successor_stations.detail: Orbital Reef was announced as a station for about 10 crew at about 500 km in a mid-inclination orbit, launched on New Glenn, operating 'before 2030'.
successor_stations.status: design phase; no current launch date
successor_stations.note: In October 2026 The Space Review described Blue Origin as low-profile but still pursuing it. https://www.thespacereview.com/article/5340/1

successor_stations.title: NASA commercial-station final RFP released
successor_stations.detail: After proposing (24 March 2026) and dropping (June 2026) a government 'core module' idea, NASA issued a final RFP on 9 October 2026, with proposals due 8 December 2026 and at least two initial awards by April 2027.
successor_stations.status: no Phase 2 awards made as of October 2026
successor_stations.note: GAO (June 2026) says NASA expects about $1.0B to $1.5B over FY2026 to FY2031, possibly enough for only one station. https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-26-107805.pdf

successor_stations.title: Tiangong (China Space Station): Tianhe core launched
successor_stations.detail: A Long March 5B launched the Tianhe core module from Wenchang, the first of three modules.

successor_stations.title: Tiangong completed with Mengtian
successor_stations.detail: Mengtian (17.9 m, about 22 t) docked and completed the three-module T-shaped station after Wentian (July 2022).

successor_stations.title: Tiangong orbit: about 384 km, 41.47 deg
successor_stations.detail: Derived: the CelesTrak element set for Tianhe (NORAD 48274) at epoch 2026-10-26 gives a mean altitude of about 384 km and inclination 41.47 deg.

successor_stations.title: Tiangong expansion to six modules
successor_stations.detail: At IAC 2023 a CAST official said a multi-functional node with six docking ports would come first, growing the station to six modules and about 180 t; no launch date has been published.

successor_stations.title: Bharatiya Antariksh Station: BAS-1 module
successor_stations.detail: India's cabinet approved the first module, BAS-1, to launch by December 2028 under an expanded Gaganyaan programme; five modules are targeted by 2035.
successor_stations.status: design phase (baseline design review done per July 2026 parliamentary reply)
successor_stations.note: Wikipedia gives a planned orbit of 400 to 450 km at 51.5 deg, but no official ISRO orbit for BAS-1 was found.

counts.title: 13,042 launched; 11,166 in orbit; 11,151 working
counts.detail: McDowell's table (updated 2026-10-26 00:51 UTC) counts 13,042 launched (20 early V3 never reached orbit), 1,876 down, 11,166 in orbit and 10,022 in their final operational shells.

counts.title: CelesTrak Starlink group: 11,109 element sets
counts.detail: CelesTrak's Starlink group held 11,109 element sets; its whole 'active' catalogue held 16,792.

gen1_shells_fcc.title: Gen1 shells (FCC 21-48)
gen1_shells_fcc.detail: The FCC set 4,408 Gen1 satellites: 1,584 at 550 km/53 deg, 1,584 at 540 km/53.2 deg, 720 at 570 km/70 deg, and 348 + 172 at 560 km/97.6 deg.

gen2_shells_fcc.title: Gen2 partial grant: 7,500 satellites
gen2_shells_fcc.detail: The FCC approved 7,500 of the 29,988 requested Gen2 satellites at 525 km/53 deg, 530 km/43 deg and 535 km/33 deg, deferring the rest.

gen2_shells_fcc.title: FCC approves 7,500 more Gen2 (total 15,000)
gen2_shells_fcc.detail: The FCC authorised another 7,500 Gen2 satellites, bringing Gen2 to 15,000, and added new shells from 340 km to 485 km plus direct-to-cell service.

shell_lowering.title: ~4,400 satellites to move from ~550 km to ~480 km during 2026
shell_lowering.detail: SpaceX's Michael Nicolls said all Starlinks at ~550 km would drop to ~480 km over 2026, so failed satellites reenter in months rather than years.

shell_lowering.title: Where the shells actually sit now
shell_lowering.detail: Derived from CelesTrak: the main clusters are ~460-470 km at 53 deg (~4,300), ~480 km at 43 deg (~3,200), ~470 km at 97 deg (~1,450), ~470 and ~570 km at 70 deg, and ~360 km at 43/53 deg (direct-to-cell).
shell_lowering.note: These are researcher-binned mean altitudes (10 km bins, clusters of 100+ satellites), not SpaceX-published shell values. The ~550 km Gen1 shell no longer appears as a major cluster, consistent with the lowering. McDowell's per-shell plots: https://planet4589.org/space/con/star/hiplots.html

filings.title: ~42,000 total requested
filings.detail: SpaceX asked the ITU for 30,000 more satellites on top of about 12,000 already FCC-approved, roughly 42,000 in all.

v3_on_starship.title: First Starlink V3 satellites deployed (Starship Flight 14)
v3_on_starship.detail: Starship reached orbit and released 26 V3 satellites (about 1 Tbps down, 160 Gbps up each), all of which made contact; a full Starship can carry up to 60.
v3_on_starship.note: On 2026-10-26 McDowell shows the 26 V3s still raising orbit (24 ascending, 2 drifting).

v3_on_starship.title: Next V3 launch (Starship Flight 15)
v3_on_starship.detail: Flight 15 had no official date as of late October 2026; unofficial trackers list NET November 2026.
v3_on_starship.note: This is a low-confidence secondary source; treat the date as unconfirmed.

starlink.projection_2030: No official SpaceX or FCC figure for 2030 was found, so it is omitted.

counts.title: ESA MASTER model: 68,450 objects >10 cm
counts.detail: ESA's 2026 report (issued 8 September 2026) estimates 68,450 objects over 10 cm (about 11,300 of them active payloads), 1.5 million from 1 to 10 cm and 230 million from 1 mm to 1 cm.
counts.note: These model estimates use the reference epoch of 1 February 2026. Earlier ESA figures (about 54,000 >10 cm, 1.2 million at 1-10 cm, 140 million <1 cm) came from an older population, so the editions differ.

counts.title: About 47,000 objects regularly tracked
counts.detail: ESA's 'Space debris by the numbers' (updated 14 October 2026) gives about 47,000 tracked objects, about 19,440 satellites in space (about 15,900 functioning) and over 17,400 t in orbit.
counts.note: The ESA page renders its numbers with JavaScript and could not be read directly; the figures come from the secondary article quoting it.

counts.title: 2025 environment trend
counts.detail: ESA reports over 300 launches and 4,000 new payloads in 2025, fewer new fragments than 2024 (which added 3,000+ catalogued fragments from propulsion breakups), and about 9.8 accidental fragmentations a year.

events.title: Fengyun-1C destroyed by Chinese ASAT test
events.detail: A ballistic interceptor destroyed the 960 kg weather satellite at about 850 km (98.6 deg), the worst LEO contamination in 50 years: 1,200+ catalogued pieces within two months and up to 35,000 estimated over 1 cm.

events.title: Iridium 33 / Cosmos 2251 collision
events.detail: The first accidental collision of two intact satellites happened at 16:56 UTC, 790 km over northern Siberia, at more than 11 km/s; 823 pieces were catalogued by the end of March 2009.

events.title: Cosmos 1408 destroyed by Russian ASAT test
events.detail: A direct-ascent missile destroyed the 1,750 kg satellite at about 490 x 465 km; more than 1,500 trackable fragments were seen, and 1,604 were catalogued by 7 March 2022.

events.title: Long March 6A upper stage breakup (Qianfan launch)
events.detail: The about 5,800 kg upper stage broke up at 17:15 UTC in an 857 x 797 km, 89 deg orbit after deploying the first 18 Qianfan satellites; 283 large fragments were catalogued by 15 September 2024.
events.note: Other counts (300+, 650+, 700+) reflect different dates and catalogues.

events.title: Intelsat 33e breaks up in GEO
events.detail: The operational Intelsat 33e broke up at about 04:30 UTC in geostationary orbit (35,773 x 35,797 km); 18 fragments were catalogued by 13 January 2025.

other_orbits.title: GPS: ~20,200 km, 6 planes, 31 operational
other_orbits.detail: GPS satellites fly in medium Earth orbit at about 20,200 km, circling twice a day in six planes; gps.gov counted 31 operational (snapshot of 3 July 2023).

other_orbits.title: GPS now: 32 in CelesTrak 'gps-ops', ~55 deg
other_orbits.detail: Derived: CelesTrak's operational-GPS group lists 32 satellites at a mean altitude of about 20,180 km and median inclination 54.9 deg.

other_orbits.title: Galileo: 23,222 km; SAT 33-34 entered service
other_orbits.detail: Galileo slots sit at 23,222 km; SAT 33 and 34 entered service in 2026, completing the L14 pair, and four first-generation satellites remain to launch.
other_orbits.note: CelesTrak's Galileo group lists 32 element sets: 30 near 23,200 km at about 55-57 deg, plus 2 in eccentric orbits (mean about 21,600 km, 49 deg). https://celestrak.org/NORAD/elements/gp.php?GROUP=galileo&FORMAT=json

other_orbits.title: GLONASS: 27 operational at ~19,100 km, ~65 deg
other_orbits.detail: Derived: CelesTrak's operational-GLONASS group lists 27 satellites at about 19,100 km with inclinations of 64-66 deg.

other_orbits.title: BeiDou: mixed MEO, IGSO and GEO
other_orbits.detail: Derived: CelesTrak's BeiDou group lists 53 satellites: 32 in MEO (~21,500 km, 54-57 deg), 12 inclined geosynchronous (IGSO) and 9 geostationary.

other_orbits.title: GEO belt altitude 35,786 km
other_orbits.detail: Geostationary satellites orbit at 35,786 km above the equator, matching Earth's rotation.

other_orbits.title: About 570 active geosynchronous satellites
other_orbits.detail: Derived: CelesTrak's 'Active Geosynchronous' group lists 569 satellites, 558 of them near one revolution per day and 368 within 1 deg of the equator.
